lmp2-1663-05-13.summary: Written two days after Don John appeared before Estremoz and the day before Évora was invested, the letter first worries about the general’s silence: the courier may have been taken. Then it announces, company by company, the cavalry leaving for the Alentejo.
lmp2-1663-05-13.en:
Count, my friend. I the King send you warm greetings, as one whom I love.

The last letter of yours received here was of the 10th of this month, and I am anxious at not having received another; it is thought the courier may have been taken. I send this one to let you know that Manuel Freire de Andrade left Coimbra on the 9th of this month, in the afternoon, with 203 horse, and writes that he will make no other halt than to mount some men who were going on foot; with him should also go everything that was lacking from the Beira relief; from this you can reckon when he may arrive there.

Of the cavalry companies of this city, that of Luís Lobo (?) […] de Agalega leaves tomorrow with 56 horse; the next day that of commissary Gonçalo da Costa leaves, and the day after Diogo Luís Ribeiro and Jorge Furtado, each taking at least 55 horse.

lmp2-1663-05-15a.summary: This is the “other letter of this same date” to which the ciphered note of 15 May refers. Partly in clear and partly in cipher, it keeps for the cipher everything that would inform the enemy: the reinforcements on the way (Beira foot and horse, Lisbon companies), the King’s plan to set up a place of arms at Setúbal or Palmela, the pay money, the help sent to Montemor. Left in clear are the greeting, the doctrine (“an army is there to fight”) and the request for a courier every day.
lmp2-1663-05-15a.en:
Count, my friend. I the King send you warm greetings, as one whom I love. Your letters of the 12th of this month have been received, in which you report what had happened up to that time and what you had learnt of the enemy; this would have caused me much greater anxiety had I not you at the head of my arms, and with you the commanders who assist you, whose valour I see passes to all the soldiers of that army and even to the inhabitants of every place, according to what I am told of their spirit; which gives me great satisfaction.

I understand that you already have there the auxiliary terços of Estremadura, except some companies of the Torres Vedras one which left later; that of the district of this city [Lisbon] is being made ready with all diligence, and although it cannot arrive for the first occasion I hope you will have, it will serve afterwards to reinforce the army.

lmp2-1663-05-15.summary: The day after Évora was invested, the King added to a long letter of the same date a note entirely in cipher apart from the greeting and the date. The main question had been “reconsidered”: if the enemy persisted and put the city in danger, Vila Flor was to gather all his forces and relieve it at all risk, “even exposing yourself to the last extremity of a battle”.
lmp2-1663-05-15.en:
Count, my friend. I the King send you warm greetings, as one whom I love.

Besides what I tell you in another letter of this same date, the main matter treated in it having been considered again, I have been pleased to resolve that, should the enemy persist in the siege of Évora and reduce that city to a dangerous state, you shall gather all the forces of that province and, with the help you expect from the others, seek to relieve it at all risk, even exposing yourself to the last extremity of a battle, for so the defence of the kingdom and my service require, given the importance of the place and the consequences that will follow from what befalls it; which I hope you will carry out with the resolution and valour that are needed.

Written in Lisbon on 15 May 1663. The King. — The Count of Castelo Melhor. — To the Count of Vila Flor.

lmp2-1663-05-26.summary: On 22 May 1663 Évora, one of the chief cities of the kingdom, surrendered to Don John Joseph of Austria. Four days later the court in Lisbon, governed by the Count of Castelo Melhor in the name of the young Afonso VI, wrote to the general of the Alentejo army, the Count of Vila Flor. The letter opens and closes in clear; the whole order is in cipher: relieve Évora “em todo o cazo e a todo o risco”, move the army without delay, show the letter to the commanders, and count on the pay money leaving in two days. Thirteen days later Vila Flor and Schomberg defeated Don John at Ameixial.

system: Simple substitution with a few homophones on Portuguese; digits and letter-like signs; three states of the key.
